extracted.intended_audience: mathematics instructors/course designers assessing student mathematical writing and presentations (undergraduate and graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and example rubrics for objectively grading student mathematical presentations (and papers), including category definitions, score-level descriptions, and meta-guidance on rubric design, weighting, and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures preparation and revision: whether the practice presentation was carefully crafted and whether revision incorporated feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score definitions (example weights shown): 20 — The practice presentation was carefully crafted. The revision took into account but was not limited to the feedback of course staff and of teammates. 15 — The practice was a work in progress, with a pre-prepared general plan and with details decided extemporaneously; the revision was limited to provided feedback; or some feedback was ignored. 10 — The practice was extemporaneous or closely followed the project paper; or the revision addressed only a few major aspects of the provided feedback. 5 — The practice was extemporaneous and the revision addressed minor aspects of the provided feedback. Also appears in a shorter form in a revised rubric: 'The practice presentation was carefully crafted. The revision took into account but was not limited to the feedback of course staff and of teammates.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Correctness and Vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Assesses mathematical progress within project scope and how convincingly phenomena are explained (rigor of proofs, strength of evidence for conjectures, clarity of problem description and insight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score definitions (example weights shown): 40 — Substantial progress is made within the available scope of the project and identified phenomena are convincingly explained (i.e., proofs are rigorous; conjectures are supported with convincing evidence). 30 — Some notable progress is made and explanations are suggested for identified phenomena (claims rigorously stated and support goes beyond a few specific examples). 20 — A good expository description of the problem and of the most interesting aspects of how it appears to behave (e.g., conjectures are stated). 10 — Description of the problem and of some immediately apparent aspects of its behavior. Note: in the revised rubric this category was removed for presentations when the associated project paper already carries the math grade, to avoid double jeopardy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicates Effectively to Target Audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluates how well the presentation/paper is crafted to be understood by the intended audience: focus, clarity, appropriate level/formality, supporting examples/figures, and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score definitions (example weights shown): 40 — The presentation is engaging and clear: tightly focused around the most interesting results; less important points de-emphasized or omitted; delivery is engaging and insightful; connections made within the talk and to other disciplines; carefully prepared and tailored to classmates. 30 — The presentation is crafted to be understood by classmates: appropriate level of difficulty and formality; examples, figures, explanations aid understanding; carefully structured; sufficient detail with clear relevance; precise language. 20 — The presenter shows his or her research using terminology and notation approximately correctly, taking sufficient care with structure, clarity, delivery, and board work to enable an expert to discern what was intended. 10 — The presenter says and writes what he or she researched without connecting to the language, knowledge, or interest of those watching (e.g., nonstandard notation without introduction, illegible writing, inaudible delivery). Note/example: Karen scored 40 on 'Communicates Effectively' yet 10 on mechanics (inaudible/illegible), highlighting potential conflicts between categories and the need for rubric refinement or re-weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical delivery elements that support understanding: board work, slides, vocal delivery, and teamwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rubric wording (20 points): Carefully structured board work complements vocal delivery by emphasizing important points and helping the audience absorb subtle points, without distracting. Slides are used as appropriate and are integrated seamlessly into the presentation. Delivery is carefully prepared. Teammates work well together. In the developmental rubric this area (board work/delivery) was de-emphasized when students were already comfortable presenting; weightings should reflect student ability and course priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The presentation is crafted to guide classmates to understanding via appropriate detail, structure, examples, figures, explanations, and precise language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rubric wording (40 points): The level of detail, difficulty, and formality are appropriate to the audience and content; the well-chosen topic, structure, examples, figures, explanations, and use of formality help the audience to understand both the problem statement and its solution; the language is precise. This category replaces broader 'Communicates Effectively' in a revised rubric that separates mechanics and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the presentation captures and holds the audience's attention and adapts to audience reactions while focusing on core results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rubric wording (20 points): The presentation is engaging and clear; tightly focused around the most interesting results while less important points are de-emphasized or omitted; delivery is engaging and insightful, with connections made both within the talk and to other disciplines; presenters adapt well to audience reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rubric weighting to reflect priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubric content and point weights should be tailored to the assignment, students, and educator priorities (e.g., precision and rigor for early proof-based courses vs insight and conventions for capstones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: A generic rubric rarely works well; successful rubrics are tailored. Within a course, different assignments may target different aspects of communication and rubrics should be adjusted. Choose weights to emphasize those priorities (example: Process 20, Clarity 40, Mechanics 20, Audience Engagement 20 in a senior lab presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting (double jeopardy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not duplicate major grading elements across separate graded artifacts (e.g., do not grade mathematical correctness fully in both the presentation and the associated project paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In the revised presentation rubric the 'Mathematical Correctness and Vision' category was removed because the project paper already carries the math grade; grading the same math content twice penalizes students unfairly and inflates math weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental rubric (design and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubric format that provides grade-level descriptions reflecting stages of learner development so the grade itself communicates meaningful feedback and next steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: reduces need for many specific comments because each grade band describes what the student has achieved and what to focus on next; links assessment with teaching. Disadvantages/challenges: difficult to create well; may not fit when brief assessment tools are required (tradeoff between developmental detail and compactness). Classroom testing and iterative revision are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric testing and refinement (Bean 'right brain/left brain' approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method for validating and refining an assessment tool by comparing holistic impressions with rubric-derived grades and iterating on discrepancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: first assign a holistic grade (A/B/etc.), then apply the rubric as objectively as feasible and compare the results. If they disagree, investigate whether the holistic grade overlooked important aspects or whether the rubric needs refinement. Classroom-testing the rubric and revising based on such comparisons is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs between developmental and simpler assessment tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the rubric's purpose is teaching, precise assessment, communication of priorities, or grading consistency; the structure/detail level should reflect that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A developmental rubric with detailed grade bands teaches students and improves consistency but is lengthy; a simpler tool (fewer categories, no level descriptions) fits on one page and leaves more room for individualized comments, but is less effective as a stand-alone teaching tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of effective mathematical communication (high-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distilled set of priorities identified by many mathematics educators: mathematical correctness, meeting assignment constraints, clarity, and being engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this general characterization as a starting point when drafting assignment-specific rubrics. These characteristics are intended to apply to both presentations and papers; they should be operationalized and weighted according to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to revise rubrics for diverse students
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubric that mirrors the development of some students may not fit all; rubrics should be revised to accommodate diverse skill profiles and to avoid contradictory signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Karen's talk was engaging but almost inaudible and illegible; a rubric that rewards engagement highly but also requires mechanics will produce conflicting scores. Solutions include splitting categories, re-weighting, or adding guidance to resolve such conflicts. Ongoing classroom use and revision is advised.
